How well do research agents answer traders' questions?

This is a set of 110 test questions for comparing Raven with general-purpose AI agents (and future specialist competitors) on the questions crypto and stock-perp traders actually ask.

Every question comes with a list of facts a good answer must get right, where to check each fact, and a simple score: 0, 1 or 2.

All agents get the same question at the same moment, and we check their answers against market data saved at that moment. That keeps the comparison fair even though prices keep moving.

Where the questions come from

40 questions come from real usage. We took questions people asked Raven, cleaned them up and made them reusable. For example, "BTC" becomes a fill-in slot, so the question still works next month.

70 were written to fill gaps. They spread the set evenly across 10 topics and three difficulty levels. Some are deliberate "trick" questions: one with a false premise, one where the data doesn't exist, one that needs an exact time.

What's new in v1.2 (Oct 16)

  • 24 regression tests from trial feedback and mobile testing, each with clear pass/fail checks (below).
  • Stress tests: 33 hard cases on their own track and calendar (see the Stress tests tab).
  • Mobile UI and product checklists, checked by hand (not scored by the judge).
  • Better comparisons: every run records the model and the app version, so we can tell whether a change in score came from the model or the app.
  • Run on ship: one command reruns the tests whenever something meaningful ships, plus a short Monday "top 5 to fix" note.

Results

Latest run: Wed Oct 21, 2026. Grok Bot answered all 110 questions using Raven's data tools (MCP) plus web search; it is shown as a fifth column next to the Oct 20 run. Oct 20, 2026: Raven, Grok, ChatGPT and Claude answered the same questions on the same day (below that). Earlier runs are kept further down: Raven vs Grok on 40 questions (Raven Oct 16, Grok Oct 13).

We graded all answers ourselves, strictly, against data saved at the moment each question was asked. Treat these numbers as a rough first look until people have double-checked them.

Method & caveats (please read)

  • What was tested: Grok Bot (a general assistant) with access to Raven's data tools over MCP, plus its own web search. This is not the Raven app: the MCP connection had no full Raven research tool, only direct data tools (prices, funding, flow, wallets, news and so on), so Grok Bot did the analysis and wrote the answers itself.
  • When: all 110 questions, one fresh task each, answered about 9:45 to 10:15 AM ET on Wed Oct 21, 2026. The other four columns are from Tue Oct 20, a different market day, so this is a comparison of answer quality, not of the same market moment.
  • How it was graded: same rubric and same strictness as Oct 20. Answers were checked against Hyperliquid candle and funding history rebuilt after the fact (no live snapshots were taken at send time), and against the cited web sources. Facts that can't be rebuilt later (order books, trade tape, some wallet states) were judged on internal consistency, sourcing, as-of times and plausibility. That makes this run somewhat easier to score well on than Oct 20 Raven, which was checked against live snapshots.
  • One grader, not blind: the grader knew which system wrote each answer. Small gaps may be noise.
  • Raven data problems during the run: several Raven data sources were degraded: the SEC filing analysis budget was used up, the daily briefing had not refreshed since Oct 15, saved wallets/signals were unavailable, the trade archive was flagged incomplete, the trades, market-context and wallet-history collectors were reported unhealthy around 10:00 AM ET, and 7-day TSLA trade data was unavailable. Grok Bot worked around these with other tools or the web, or said so.
  • Light contamination: eight answers (Q53, 56, 57, 59, 66, 93, 94, 97) were edited after they were first written, to remove facts carried over from earlier questions. They are flagged.
  • Other notes: answer times were not recorded reliably, so the 4-minute time limit was not applied. Saving alerts was not allowed in this run, so AS-01 was scored on whether the exact conditions and delivery were stated. For follow-up questions only the last message was sent, which cost points on AS-10. XM-03 is excluded for everyone (broken question); PN-02 is flagged as a likely faulty question.
  • Answer text: unlike Oct 20, Grok Bot's answers are published (click "Grok Bot + MCP answer" in each row). Wallet addresses are shortened, and file paths and emails are removed.

What stood out

  • Grok Bot + MCP scored highest on both the compared set and the core 40, with no 0 scores. Raven's own data (funding, flow, wallets, books) gave it exact numbers, and it usually stated the universe, time window and as-of time.
  • Where it lost points: screens and rankings that were only partly run (AS-03 skipped smaller builder exchanges and missed the day's top gainer; AS-09 left part of the screen unchecked; OF-05 missed one of the most active markets), missing official release or publish times (PN-04, PN-05, PN-06, PN-10), and one conflicting token-unlock answer (CC-06).
  • Fair-comparison warning: different market day, a grader who knew the source, and after-the-fact references. Treat the gap as a signal, not a precise ranking.

core 40		Price moves & newsWhy did KNTQ fall from about 0.45 to 0.28 in early October 2026?11112
Grok Bot + MCP: Gives a release time (8:01 ET) from a secondary blog, not the official schedule; high/low after release not checkable; post-release move incomplete.
Raven: Cause (kPoints end / paid claim) matches; no official announcement time; high/low not checked against spot DEX history.
Grok: Cause (kPoints end, 50M KNTQ paid claim at $0.26, 10-day window) matches; high/low from reports (not checkable vs spot DEX history); no announcement time.
ChatGPT: Cause (kPoints end, 50M KNTQ at $0.26, 10-day window) matches; 0.42-0.45 -> 0.28 range from reports (not checkable vs spot DEX history); no announcement time ('reported on October 2').
Claude: Cause (kPoints end Oct 1, 50M KNTQ paid claim at $0.26, 10-day window, no lockup) matches the Kinetiq blog; range checked against reports (ATH $0.4515 Oct 1, ~$0.281 low; not checkable vs spot DEX history); announcement time given (8:01 a.m. ET Oct 1, outlet-reported) but the official post time could not be verified.
Grok Bot + MCP answer
**Short answer:** KNTQ (Kinetiq's governance token) dropped on **Oct 1, 2026** because Kinetiq ended its kPoints program with a **paid claim instead of a free airdrop**. kPoints holders got the right to *buy* a combined **50M KNTQ at a fixed $0.26**, about 35% below spot, with **no lockup**. The market priced in a large block of discounted, immediately sellable supply. **What happened (per reports):** - **Oct 1, 8:01 AM ET:** Kinetiq said the final kPoints had been distributed (36.8M kPoints over 46 weeks). Eligible holders could claim 50M KNTQ at $0.26 in USDC during a 10-day window. Unclaimed tokens go back to the Kinetiq Foundation. Kinetiq's post said KNTQ was "around $0.40" at the time ([Kinetiq blog, Oct 1 2026](https://kinetiq.xyz/blog/kntq-kpoints-claim)). - **Price:** The Defiant (CoinGecko data) puts KNTQ at about **$0.422** just before the announcement. It fell to an intraday low near **$0.281** around 10:05 AM ET (about −33%), then recovered to about **$0.325** by 12:09 AM ET Oct 2 (−23%). HYPE fell only about 1.8% over the same period, so this was a KNTQ-specific move, not the broader market ([The Defiant via cryptonews.net, Oct 2 2026 04:42 UTC](https://cryptonews.net/news/defi/33528205/); [TechFlow](https://techflowpost.com/en-US/newsletter/138608); [KuCoin flash](https://www.kucoin.com/news/flash/kinetiq-ends-kpoints-program-kntq-price-drops-23-after-token-sale-launch)). - **Why it hurt:** Farmers expected free tokens and got a purchase option. The discount gave claimants an incentive to buy at $0.26 and sell. Up to $13M of new float with no vesting created a supply overhang. There was also criticism of how it was communicated (e.g., DeFi Dad said the team should have said upfront that points were a discounted call option). **Small correction to the premise:** Reported pre-announcement prices were about **$0.40–0.42**, not $0.45. The about-$0.28 level was an **intraday low**, not where the price settled; it bounced to about $0.32 within a day. The claim window ran to about **Oct 10/11**. **Coverage note:** KNTQ is a spot token and isn't listed as a Hyperliquid perp in Raven's market registry (no match as of 13:45 UTC Oct 21). Raven's news feed also had no KNTQ posts in the last 30 days. So this answer relies on web reporting, not Raven market data. Prices are as reported by those outlets, not independently checked tick-by-tick.

**Short answer: there's no real 24h brief to give, because xyz:RELIANCE isn't actually trading.** The market exists on Hyperliquid (Trade.xyz HIP-3 deployer), but it hasn't opened. Columbus Day (Oct 12) has already passed, and stocks were open that day too. **How stock perps (e.g., trade[XYZ] `xyz:` markets on Hyperliquid) behave when the underlying is closed** - **The perps keep trading 24/7.** Only the *reference price* changes. trade[XYZ] takes external stock prices 24/5, from Sunday 8:05 PM ET to Friday 8:00 PM ET, covering pre-market, regular hours, post-market and overnight via Blue Ocean ATS (docs.trade.xyz/perpetuals/markets/stocks/us). - **When no external price is available** (weekends, and in practice full exchange holidays like Thanksgiving when the US sessions don't run), the oracle switches to **internal pricing**. It starts from the last external price and drifts toward the perp's own order-book impact bid/ask through a ~30-minute EMA. Each update can move it by only a limited fraction (docs.trade.xyz/perpetuals/mechanics/oracle-price). When external pricing resumes, the oracle **snaps back to the live external price on the next tick**. - **What that means in practice:** 1. **Price discovery happens on the perp itself.** Holiday or weekend moves reflect perp traders' flow, not the stock. Thin books make it easier for a few large orders to push price. 2. **Liquidity is usually thinner**, with wider spreads and less depth, so slippage and stop-hunts are more likely. 3. **Gap or reopen risk:** if news hits while the stock is closed and the perp has drifted, the oracle can jump when the cash market reopens. This affects funding (which references the oracle) and can cause liquidations. 4. **Funding** is based on the mark/oracle premium, so a one-sided holiday perp can build up a premium or discount that then collapses at the reopen. - **On days like Veterans Day (Nov 11)**, stocks trade normally, so stock perps should behave as on any normal session. Only Treasuries are closed, which can make rate-sensitive moves a bit thinner. **Caveats:** trade[XYZ]'s docs describe the weekend closure explicitly. I did not find a holiday-specific page, so applying internal pricing on Thanksgiving is inferred from "external inputs unavailable." Other builder venues (non-`xyz:` prefixes) may use different oracle rules. Q59		Funding ratesHow often is funding paid on Hyperliquid and is it capped?22222
Grok Bot + MCP: Correct.
Raven: Hourly payment and cap correct.
Grok: Hourly settlement and 4%/h cap correct (plus baseline 0.00125%/h).
ChatGPT: Hourly settlement and ±4%/h cap correct; docs cited.
Claude: Hourly settlement and 4%/h cap correct; docs cited.
Grok Bot + MCP answer
**Hyperliquid pays funding every hour, and yes, it's capped at 4% per hour** in either direction. The cap and the interval are the same for every asset (Hyperliquid docs). **How it works** - **Hourly settlement:** the formula produces an 8-hour rate, like a CEX, and each hour **1/8 of it** is paid. It's peer-to-peer between longs and shorts, and Hyperliquid takes no fee on funding. - **The formula:** Funding = average Premium Index + clamp(interest rate − premium, −0.05%, +0.05%). - The premium is sampled every 5 seconds and averaged over the hour. It's based on impact bid/ask prices versus the oracle, where the oracle is a weighted median of CEX spot prices. - The interest component is fixed at **0.01% per 8h = 0.00125% per hour** (≈11% APR, paid by longs to shorts). So when the perp trades near the oracle, funding settles at exactly 0.00125%/h. For example, Raven shows BTC's current hourly funding estimate at exactly 0.00125% (14:00 UTC Oct 21). - If the perp trades above the oracle, funding is positive and longs pay shorts. If it trades below, funding is negative and shorts pay longs. - **Payment amount:** position size × **oracle price** × funding rate. It uses the oracle price, not the mark price. - **The 4%/hour cap:** this is far looser than typical CEX caps. Extreme readings are possible in squeezes and in thin markets. **HIP-3 / builder-deployed perps (e.g. `xyz:` stock perps)** use a more responsive mid-based premium formula. Deployers can set their own interest rate and a funding multiplier. For example, Raven's settled funding for xyz:NVDA shows hourly settlements (6 of 6 from 09:00 to 14:00 UTC today) at a **0.000625%/h** baseline, half the native rate, with a brief negative print of −0.000105% at 11:00 UTC. They still pay hourly under the same 4%/h cap. **Comparison:** Binance and Bybit usually settle every 8h (some pairs every 4h or 1h) and have tighter, pair-specific caps. Hyperliquid's hourly settlement means you pay or receive in smaller, more frequent amounts. Sources: Hyperliquid docs, Funding (https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/trading/funding, fetched Oct 21, 2026). Live examples: Raven market context BTC (~14:00 UTC) and Raven settled_funding xyz:NVDA (6h window ending 14:00 UTC Oct 21, 2026).

Oct 20, 2026: Raven vs Grok vs ChatGPT vs Claude

Same day, same questions, four services: Raven (the real app) and three general AI chat apps: Grok, ChatGPT and Claude. Each answer gets 0, 1 or 2 points, and the percentage is points earned out of points possible.

Method & caveats (please read)

  • How Raven was asked: through the Raven app itself, on a test account, using the model gpt-6.1-sol. Every question got a fresh chat. Raven ran from 10:41 AM to 1:04 PM ET.
  • How the other three were asked: using ordinary paid consumer subscriptions, typed into each app in a web browser, with a fresh chat for every question. Each question went to all three apps within about a minute of each other, between 10:45 AM and 3:45 PM ET.
  • Settings: ChatGPT Plus with High effort, Claude Fable 5.1 on Medium, Grok in Expert mode. Web search was left at each app's default.
  • Which questions: only questions 1 to 102 were asked in the apps. We stopped at 3:50 PM ET so every answer came during US stock-market hours. Raven answered all 110 (75.5% on all 110).
  • Left out: XM-03 is excluded for everyone because the question itself was broken (a fill-in blank was never filled). That leaves 101 questions for the comparison. PN-02 is probably also a faulty question (it asks about a market, xyz:RBLX, that isn't listed). It is still scored, and flagged.
  • One grader, not blind: one person graded every answer and could see which service wrote it. Small gaps may be noise.
  • Different moments: the apps answered later in the day than Raven, so prices and news had moved. Each answer was checked against the market at the time it was asked, but the services did not all see the same market.
  • Links lost: the app answers were saved as plain text, so their clickable source links were lost. Two questions that depend on links (PN-10, FE-11) are flagged. Without the penalties for missing links and times, the scores would be Grok 70.8%, ChatGPT 67.3%, Claude 58.9%.
  • Claude's extra tools: Claude sometimes tried to use the tester's linked computer or browser to fetch data. Some of those permission prompts were declined, and then it often could not get the data.
  • Clarifying questions: if a service answered with a question back ("which exchange do you mean?"), that reply was scored as its answer.
  • Follow-ups: two questions meant as conversations (PN-05, WA-03) only had their first message sent in the apps. Answer-time limits were not enforced for the apps.

What stood out

  • Raven scored highest overall and on the core 40. Its biggest leads were on wallets, buying & selling flow and the 24-hour market summary, where its own live Hyperliquid data helps.
  • Raven was not best everywhere: ChatGPT and Grok scored higher on upcoming events and on perps vs stocks.
  • The general apps often used other exchanges' data (or out-of-date prices) for Hyperliquid questions. Stale prices shown as current scored 0.
  • Claude often couldn't reach Hyperliquid's data from its own workspace. It sometimes offered a script or a list of tools instead of an answer, and those scored 0 or 1.

What we learned

  • Good at simple lookups (price, funding, spread) and spotting false premises.
  • Weak at anything needing a full history of trades: who's buying and how much over the last hour. Public data only shows the last few trades.
  • Honest: it admitted missing data in 20 of 21 cases where it should.

When each service was run

Questions are sent during US stock-market hours (9:30 am – 4:00 pm New York time on trading days), so every service sees the same live market. That includes the crypto questions.

Regression tests

Each test passes only if every check holds. Most come from trial feedback; the ones marked "keep" protect things that already work well.

Raven, Fri Oct 16 (market hours): 8 pass, 14 fail, 2 not run. The main misses: answers too slow for the time targets, topics we don't cover don't fail fast yet, answers to identity questions still reveal internal setup details (we are not publishing those details), and answers don't suggest Following, ratings or insider features. Two follow-up tests weren't run because the test connection can't send a message mid-answer yet.

Stress tests

33 extra-hard questions, kept separate from the main benchmark.

The stress tests are their own track. They are not part of the 110-question benchmark and they don't change the headline score. They are deliberately tough edge cases, many full of traps: false premises, look-alike tickers, time-zone cut-offs, weekend market reopens.

Because many only make sense at a particular moment (for example, right as a market reopens on a Sunday evening), they run on their own calendar. Every service is asked within the same 15 minutes, and they are scored 0, 1 or 2 the same way as the main set.

"Any session" tests can run at any time the US stock market is open, so they are being run in weekday batches from Oct 19 to Oct 30.

Summary: any-session pool (22 tests, Oct 19-27)

Raven scored 35 out of 44 (about 80%) across the 22 tests that can run in any market session. It got full marks (2) on 13 tests and partial credit (1) on 9, with no zeros on its final answers. Only Raven was tested: the ChatGPT and Claude connections are not built yet and there is no Grok connection for scheduled runs, so there is no side-by-side comparison on this track. Each test was scored once by a single grader (Grok), not blind. For SKHX vs SKHY funding (ST-04) and the silver crash (ST-15), the score is from the Oct 27 re-run, because both timed out on their first try. Memory perps, every deployer (ST-01) was asked three times and scored 1, 0 and 2, so it counts as 1 here.

Where Raven did well. It was strong on venue rules and contract specs, and it checked them against the venue's own documents instead of guessing (ST-03, ST-23, ST-24, ST-25). It caught false or outdated premises: it said Samsung funding was positive, not negative, when the question was asked in Chinese (ST-32), and it caught a16z's updated figures (ST-26). When sources disagreed, it named the measure behind each number instead of averaging them (ST-27).

Where it lost points. It was weaker at explaining things that depend on timing and on other markets: Korean versus US trading hours and the KRW conversion (ST-04, ST-13), splitting a move by session, and the knock-on effect in crypto on the weekend after the silver crash (ST-15, ST-18). It often used a single snapshot when the question needed realized averages or the wider context, such as paying-side averages, normalizing gold costs and the forecast request, where it gave a bare 50% with no funding, positioning or catalyst dates (ST-19, ST-20, ST-31). It also gave different answers to the same question: ST-01 ranged from 0 to 2 across three tries.

Reliability. Two answers timed out at the 210-second limit on their first run. Both answered in about 75 and 125 seconds on the re-run with a longer limit. In one fresh chat, Raven referred to "my earlier answer" (ST-28), which may mean context is carrying over between sessions and is worth checking.

Housekeeping. Several test notes went out of date during the run and should be updated before the next round (ST-12, ST-21, ST-23, ST-26, ST-27, ST-29). The dated tests (ST-05, ST-16 and ST-33 so far, and more through Nov 18) continue on their own calendar and are not part of this total.

**The weekend move was a round trip, not a trend: xyz:XYZ100 slid into Saturday, then repriced upward within minutes of the US index-futures reopen on Sunday evening.** - xyz:XYZ100 fell from a Friday high of $29,755 (16 Oct, 14:48 UTC) to $28,935 on Saturday at 21:31 UTC (-2.8%), a move the perp priced itself since the cash index was closed. It then jumped $28,973 → $29,335 between 22:11 and 22:30 UTC on Sunday and extended to $29,601 by early Monday. Latest mark $29,524, +1.7% versus the prior-day reference of $29,031. - The trigger was macro, not market-specific. US equity futures reopened Sunday 22:00 UTC higher as "Black Monday" crash fears faded — S&P 500 +0.2%, Nasdaq 100 +0.2% ([tradfi_t3 post, 18 Oct 22:07 UTC](https://t.me/tradfi_t3/238085)) — then extended to Nasdaq 100 futures +1% and S&P futures above 7,700 ([19 Oct 00:58 UTC](https://t.me/tradfi_t3/238089)). The sibling xyz:SP500 perp jumped 7,624 → 7,666 at 22:04 UTC, confirming a venue-wide index repricing. - Weekend weakness showed as a discount: the perp traded up to ~0.33% below its oracle near Saturday's low with funding briefly negative. Since the gap it sits near oracle with funding at +0.000625%/hr and base OI down 8.7% over three days to 10,120 contracts ($299m). Counterpoint: three days net -0.40%, so this is a recovery to Friday levels rather than a new high; the rally came with shrinking open interest, not fresh positioning. **Bitget’s 80% drop was a stock-split adjustment, not an 80% loss; Hyperliquid’s 45% drop was an oracle malfunction that caused real liquidations.** ### Bitget: five times the tokens, one-fifth the price Bitget converted each **preSPAX token into five preSPCX tokens** on **28 May 2026**, reopening trading at 09:00 UTC. Its [27 May official notice](https://www.bitget.com/support/articles/12560603884442) explicitly says total holding value remained unchanged, excluding market fluctuations. For example, **one token worth $900 became five worth $180 each—still $900**. The split itself did not cost holders money; subsequent trading losses are a separate matter. ### Hyperliquid: incorrect pricing triggered forced exits This affected **Ventuals’ SPACEX-USDH synthetic perpetual**, not actual SpaceX shares. [Unchained’s 29 May report](https://unchainedcrypto.com/spacex-pre-ipo-contract-on-hyperliquid-ventuals-crashes-45-on-faulty-oracle-data-liquidating-hundreds/) attributes the malfunction to Notice.co’s feed mishandling SpaceX’s five-for-one split. Incorrect oracle data moved the liquidation mark and triggered leveraged-position liquidations. **Liquidated traders suffered real realized losses:** a subsequent price recovery does not restore a position already forcibly closed. But the reported liquidation *notional* is not the same as dollars of customer equity lost, and not every holder lost 45%. Ventuals promised compensation within 48 hours, according to [The Block, 29 May](https://www.theblock.co/post/402991/ventuals-to-compensate-traders-after-pre-ipo-spacex-perps-plunge-45-on-hyperliquid). **These sources do not establish that compensation was actually paid or everyone was made whole.**

[Hyperliquid’s documentation](https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/trading/margining) makes cross-DEX sharing dependent on account mode. The lesson is to assess **joint downside, total leverage and margin separation**, rather than assume a gold perp behaves like unleveraged bullion. **Qualification:** these snapshots do not prove crypto selling caused metals selling, establish permanent correlation, or measure the later 31 January cascade. ST-25Deployer shutdown2026-10-23 11:16 ET (Fri)
Session: Market hours (regular)		–––2
Raven (score 2)
**A shutdown announcement does not itself close your positions or erase your margin.** What matters is whether the deployer actually settles its markets onchain. Under [Hyperliquid’s official HIP-3 rules](https://hyperliquid.gitbook.io/hyperliquid-docs/hyperliquid-improvement-proposals-hips/hip-3-builder-deployed-perpetuals): - **Open positions:** The deployer can invoke `haltTrading` for each market. That cancels all outstanding orders and settles open positions at the **current mark price**—not your entry price, necessarily the last trade, or a price promised in the announcement. Your resulting profit or loss is realized; positions do not automatically migrate to another deployer. - **Margin:** Settlement removes the margin requirement for the closed position. What remains is your account equity after realized losses/profits and applicable funding or fees—not necessarily your original deposit. Remaining collateral stays in the protocol account rather than becoming the deployer’s shutdown payout. Transfer availability depends on the collateral token, account configuration and any remaining obligations. - **Before settlement:** Unless the markets have actually been settled, you can still have price exposure, funding obligations and liquidation risk. A closing website is not the same as an onchain settlement. - **Deployer stake:** It is separate from your margin. It is **not a reimbursement fund**: the documentation says slashed stake is burned, not distributed to affected traders. I haven’t verified your deployer’s announcement or settlement status. **Which deployer is it, and can you share the announcement link?** That will let me distinguish a frontend closure from a market settlement and check the stated timing.
Raven (2): Explained that the deployer halts each market and positions settle at mark, that settlement isn't a normal close at your price, that margin left after realized P&L stays in your account, and that until the market is actually halted you still carry price, funding and liquidation risk. 1. **They do not track exactly the same security.** xyz:SKHX tracks one SK Hynix common share listed in Seoul. xyz:SKHY tracks one Nasdaq ADS, representing **one-tenth of a common share**, according to [trade.xyz’s specifications](https://docs.trade.xyz/perpetuals/specifications-and-schedules/pre-ipo-specification-index). That ratio affects the price unit—not mechanically the funding percentage. 2. **Funding is calculated independently for each order book against its own oracle.** trade.xyz uses the hourly average premium of impact bid/ask prices relative to the oracle, then applies an interest component, a clamp and a funding multiplier. Different liquidity and trading pressure therefore produce different rates—even for closely related securities. It is **not simply the current mark–oracle spread**. See [funding mechanics](https://docs.trade.xyz/perpetuals/mechanics/funding). 3. **The current gap is consistent with that mechanism.** The snapshot shows much higher positive funding for xyz:SKHX. xyz:SKHY’s rate matches the **0.000625%/hour neutral interest component** implied by the documented 0.5 multiplier. Both positive rates mean longs pay shorts; the snapshot does not establish traders’ motives. **Evidence:** Hyperliquid context received October 27, 2026, 15:19:37 UTC; fresh, complete retained minute coverage over approximately 14:49–15:19 UTC. Rates are estimates, not settled payments. Contract definitions and calculation verified in trade.xyz documentation. _Data as of 2026-10-27 15:19 UTC._

How answers are scored

Each answer gets 0, 1 or 2:

2
Correct and complete. Every key fact is right, sources and times are given, and missing data is admitted rather than guessed.
1
Partly right. On topic with nothing made up, but something is missing, out of date, or unsourced.
0
Wrong or no answer. A key fact is wrong or made up, a false premise is accepted, or the agent failed or ran out of time.

The checking process

  1. Fill in the blanks. Swap placeholders like {TICKER} for real values, and replace any that have gone stale.
  2. Ask every agent at once. Send each question to all agents at the same moment, and record how long each takes and whether it failed. Each agent gets 4 minutes.
  3. Save the real answer key. Within a minute of sending, pull the true numbers from the original sources: the exchange's own data, SEC filings, official announcements, blockchain explorers and official calendars.
  4. Grade without names. Hide which agent wrote each answer, check each fact against the saved numbers, then give 0, 1 or 2.
  5. Double-check. An AI grader can do the first pass. People re-check a sample of one in five, plus every 0 and every trick question.

How close is "correct"?

Prices count as correct within 0.5% of the saved value. Percent changes are allowed 0.3 points. Official event times must be within a minute, using the time the source published it, not when a news channel reposted it. Each question lists its own allowance.

Also tracked for every run

Did it cite sources? Did it give times? Did it admit missing data? Did it keep track of earlier messages in the conversation? How often did agents fail or time out? How long did a typical answer take, and how long did the slowest one in ten take?

How this fits the Eval Desk

The Eval Desk gives each answer a 0–100 quality score from seven weighted ratings (usefulness, trading relevance, unique information, evidence, honesty about uncertainty, answering the question, clarity). Anything flagged as a serious error is capped at 40.

We treat every "automatic zero" item as a serious error, so the two scores line up. Roughly, a 2 here is a desk score of 75 or more, and a 0 is 40 or less. The questions can be imported into the desk 50 at a time.

Product feedback

From trial feedback

  • Long research runs need a time limit and should show a partial answer first.
  • Questions on topics we don't cover (A/H share spreads, stock options) should get a quick, honest "not covered".
  • Follow-up messages sent while an answer is running must not be dropped.
  • Always show how fresh the data is, and flag lags.
  • Answers about identity must never show internal details.
  • Add a fixed "what can Raven do" card in English and Chinese.
  • Use an RWA-perps example in onboarding.
  • Suggest Following, ratings and insider features inside answers.
  • Working well: fast simple lookups, finding perps by name, Chinese replies, keeping facts separate from guesses.

Austin's feedback: mobile

  • Chats scroll sideways in the mobile browser.
  • Charts are hard to read on a phone.
  • Tapping a bar should show its value.

Austin's feedback: product

  • Rankings everywhere, with time-range selectors (1D/1W/1M/YTD) (product UX)
  • Bubble charts for insider and Congress trades (product UX)
  • Checkboxes instead of toggles for filters (product UX)
  • Tickers on bank-upgrade headlines and an upgrades ranking (data)
  • Price-target gap ranking (target vs price) (data)
  • Hide or fill empty initiations / reiterations sections (product UX)
  • News categories more granular than 'TradFi' (data)
  • Macro: calendar view and relative times ('in 2 h') (product UX)
  • Explain SEC form types in catalysts (8-K, 10-Q, Form 4 …) (product UX)
  • Connect related company events (earnings ↔ filings ↔ ratings) (data)
  • Wallet net-buy rankings (data)
  • Simpler filing insights that say why they matter (backend/agent)
  • Add equities and commodities to Markets › Following (product UX)

What Raven should cover next

  1. Order flow & wallets, deeper (net-buy rankings, labelled whale cohorts, flow by hour with as-of): Biggest log theme (wallets 33/172 = 19%); flow answers cite sources only 50% of the time; baseline weakest on flow (38%) and wallets (63%), so a general assistant can't do this well
  2. RWA/stock perps across all deployers, with session clocks and corporate actions (dividends, splits): Same tickers listed by several deployers with different prices and liquidity; stress tests 1–14 focus here; trial users liked lookup by name
  3. Catalysts linked to tickers (earnings, rating changes, insider/Form 4, SEC filings explained): No trial user found Following/insider/ratings; baseline "Upcoming events" 63%; Austin's product list (PX-04/05/09/10/12)
  4. Asia / Chinese users: Chinese answers + capability card; decide on A/H spreads: Chinese replies work; ~4 trial users asked capabilities first; an A/H question spun 12 min
  5. Alerts & monitoring: alerts_watch in logs; a gap in the stress set; pairs with Following
  6. Not now: stock options: Asked in trial, but no data and a large build

What's still missing

Known gaps

  • The fact checklists are first drafts and haven't been tested on real runs.
  • Some example values will go out of date and need swapping.
  • Only 17 of the 100 questions are easy.
  • General AI agents can't set alerts, so those questions mostly test whether an agent is honest about that.
  • The usage logs are small: 172 conversations.

Next steps

  • Build the tool that saves the answer key at send time.
  • Connect Raven, GPT and Claude, and do a first full run.
  • Check the AI grader against human grades.
  • Add checks for known Raven issues: unclear chart labels, delayed trade data, wrong news times, dropped follow-up messages.
  • Rerun weekly and after every change.
